h1: The 6 Best Blenders Under $200 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: the 6 best blenders under $200, from Ninja pitchers to nutribullet cups, compared on wattage, capacity and use case.
summary: The Ninja BN751 is the best blender under $200 for most homes, since it pairs a 72oz pitcher with two 24oz to-go cups and three Auto-iQ programs. The Ninja Mega Kitchen System adds an 8-cup processor bowl for cooks who want two appliances in one. Solo smoothie drinkers can stop at the nutribullet Pro+.
intro: Peak watts are the number printed biggest on every blender box, and they are the worst way to choose one. What you put in the jar decides which machine is right. A 72oz pitcher is silly for a single morning smoothie, while a personal cup is hopeless the day you want soup or frozen drinks for a table of friends.

All six blenders here share the $100 to $200 price bucket, so we ranked them on container sizes, motor rating, included programs and extra functions from the spec sheets. We left out the pricier Ninja kitchen system because it sits above the $200 line, and we note where a wattage figure is a peak rating.

products.name: Ninja BN751 Professional Plus DUO Blender, 1400 Peak Watts, 72oz + 2x24oz Cups
products.verdict: A full pitcher and two to-go cups from one base.
products.description:
The Ninja BN751 Professional Plus DUO packs 1400 peak watts behind a 72oz pitcher, adds two 24oz to-go cups and runs three Auto-iQ programs that handle the blending and pausing for you. It lands in the $100 to $200 bucket.

It tops the ranking because one base covers a family batch on Sunday and a single-serve smoothie on Monday, which no pitcher-only model manages. The BN701 below gives up the cups for a simpler setup, so the price you pay for the leader is mostly extra parts to store.

Buy it if your household blends in both sizes. Remember the 1400 figure is peak watts, not continuous power, so judge performance on programs and capacity, not the headline. Skip it if you only ever blend one large batch.
products.idealFor: Households blending both batches and single servings.
products.skipIf: You only ever blend one large batch.

products.name: Ninja Mega Kitchen System, 1500W, 72oz Pitcher, 8-Cup, BL770
products.verdict: Blender and 8-cup food processor on one 1500W base.
products.description:
The Ninja Mega Kitchen System BL770 puts a 1500W motor under a 72oz pitcher and an 8-cup food processor bowl, making it a blender and chopper on one base. It also sits in the $100 to $200 bucket.

Second place follows since it trades the BN751's Auto-iQ programs and to-go cups for the processor, and the listing names no preset programs. The 1500W motor is the strongest here, which counts for dense mixtures. The cost is counter footprint, since the extra bowl and blades demand more storage.

Buy it if you want to chop vegetables, mix dough-like items and blend from the same machine, replacing a separate processor. Skip it if your counter or cabinet space is tight, or if you want presets and personal cups, which the BN751 delivers.
products.idealFor: Cooks who want a blender and processor in one.

products.name: Ninja Professional Plus Blender, Auto-iQ, 1400W, 72oz Pitcher, BN701
products.verdict: Simple batch blending with Auto-iQ presets.
products.description:
The Ninja Professional Plus BN701 pairs a 1400W motor with a 72oz pitcher and Auto-iQ preset programs. There are no cups and no processor, which keeps the setup uncluttered. It is priced in the $100 to $200 bucket.

It slides under the BN751 because that model gives you the same pitcher and presets plus two cups for the same bucket. It stays above the BR201AMZ because it has 200W more power. The honest tradeoff here is single-purpose simplicity: fewer parts to wash and store.

Buy it if you blend family batches only and prefer a clean counter with minimal accessories. Skip it if you want to-go cups, because nothing in the box handles a single portion. If you can accept the clutter, the BN751 is simply the better buy at the same price.

products.name: nutribullet SmartSense Blender Combo, 1400W, 64oz Pitcher, 32oz & 24oz Cups
products.verdict: A pitcher-plus-cups setup outside the Ninja line.
products.description:
The nutribullet SmartSense Blender Combo is the best option outside the Ninja line. It lists a 1400W motor, a 64oz pitcher, 32oz and 24oz cups and five-speed SmartSense control, and costs in the $100 to $200 bucket.

Fourth position reflects that the pitcher is smaller than the Ninja's 72oz and the listing names no preset programs. What you get instead is a larger 32oz to-go cup and manual speed control, which suits cooks who like to steer the texture themselves rather than trust a preset.

Buy it if you prefer the nutribullet brand and want a pitcher plus cups in one box. Skip it if you want the largest pitcher or hands-off presets. For a family that regularly blends big batches, the extra 8oz of Ninja pitcher capacity is easy to miss until you need it.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want pitcher and cups from nutribullet.

products.name: Ninja Professional Blender 2.0, 1200W, Auto-iQ, 72oz Pitcher, BR201AMZ
products.verdict: A 72oz pitcher with Auto-iQ and no extras.
products.description:
The Ninja Professional 2.0 BR201AMZ is the plain version: a 1200W motor, a 72oz pitcher and Auto-iQ preset programs, with no cups or extras. It stays in the $100 to $200 bucket.

It sits fifth because the BN701 offers 200W more power for the same price tier, and the specs are otherwise similar. That gap makes it hard to recommend over the model above. What it does well is keep things simple, with a big pitcher, presets and nothing else to wash.

Buy it if you find it discounted within the bucket and want a pitcher blender for batches without frills. Skip it if you want cups or a processor bowl, since neither is included. Like the other Ninja listings, check whether the wattage on the page is a peak figure before assuming it handles ice and frozen fruit effortlessly.
products.idealFor: Buyers wanting a plain pitcher blender.

products.name: nutribullet Pro+ Personal Blender 1200W, 32oz & 24oz Cups
products.description:
The nutribullet Pro+ is a personal blender with a 1200W motor, two to-go cups at 32oz and 24oz, a pulse function and auto shut-off. It is also listed in the $100 to $200 bucket.

The bottom slot comes from the fact that there is no pitcher, so batch jobs such as soups, sauces or drinks for guests are out. The upside is a small footprint and a dead-simple workflow: blend in the cup, screw on a lid and go. For one person, nothing more is needed.

Buy it for solo smoothies and protein shakes where counter space is limited. Skip it if you cook for several people. At this price, the BN751 offers both personal cups and a family-size pitcher, so the Pro+ makes sense mainly for buyers who truly want the smallest, simplest machine.

whatMatters.detail: Watts describe motor power, and a peak figure is a short burst rather than sustained output. More power helps with ice and fibrous vegetables. Read whether the listing says peak or continuous. Several Ninja models quote peak watts, with the BL770 at 1500W and the BR201AMZ at 1200W.

Container size decides how much one blend yields. A 72oz pitcher feeds a family, while 24oz and 32oz cups suit one person. Buying the wrong size wastes money and counter space. Check capacities in ounces on the listing. The BN751 offers both, and the Pro+ offers cups only.

Auto-iQ is Ninja's preset system that blends and pauses on a programmed cycle, which helps beginners get consistent results. It matters if you want hands-off smoothies and crushed ice. Look for named presets in the title or bullets. The BN751 lists three, and the BL770 lists none.

An 8-cup processor bowl lets the same base chop, mix and shred, replacing a separate appliance. It matters if you cook from scratch. Check the bowl size and that it is included. The BL770 is the only model here with one, and it brings a larger footprint.

Counter footprint covers the space and storage a blender needs, including extra cups and bowls. Tall pitchers may not fit under cabinets. Check dimensions on the listing and measure your shelf. Kitchen systems like the BL770 take far more room than the nutribullet Pro+.

faq.a: Not necessarily. Several Ninja listings state peak watts, a short burst rating, so the 1400 on the BN751 is not continuous power. Read whether the figure is peak or continuous, then compare features and capacity.

faq.q: What is the most common buying mistake?
faq.a: Buying a 72oz pitcher for single servings or a personal cup for family batches. Match the container to the number of people you serve. The BN751 solves this by including both a pitcher and two cups.

faq.q: Is the BL770 worth it over the BN751?
faq.a: If you want the 8-cup processor bowl, yes. The BL770 also has a 1500W motor. If you prefer to-go cups and Auto-iQ presets, the BN751 is the better match for most homes.

faq.q: Do these come with to-go cups?
faq.a: The BN751, the nutribullet SmartSense combo and the nutribullet Pro+ include cups. The BN701 and BR201AMZ are pitcher only, so they suit batch blending but not grab-and-go smoothies.

faq.q: How should I clean a pitcher blender?
faq.a: Rinse the pitcher right after use and check the manual for dishwasher safety. Avoid letting thick mixtures dry on the blade. Blenders such as the BN701 and BR201AMZ clean fastest because they have fewer parts.

faq.q: Why is the Ninja kitchen system BN801 not included?
faq.a: Its price bucket is $200 to $500, above this ranking's $200 limit. That is why the Ninja BN801 kitchen system does not appear here, even though it is a close sibling of the BL770.

finalTake: For most households the Ninja BN751 is the blender to buy under $200, because it handles both family batches and single servings with three Auto-iQ programs. The BL770 is the pick for cooks who want a processor too, and the nutribullet Pro+ suits solo smoothie drinkers. Choose by container size and extra function first, and never by the peak watts printed on the box.
